title: Moving to the Netherlands with a teenager: school options
desc: A teen of 12 to 18 can join an ISK, a regular school, a bilingual (tto) or an international school. School is compulsory to 16, and to 18 without a diploma.
h1: We are moving with a 12 to 18 year old: what are the school options?
lede: A teenager who speaks little Dutch usually starts in an ISK, then moves to regular secondary school or mbo. Bilingual (tto) and international schools are other options. School is compulsory until the end of the school year in which your child turns 16. Without a havo, vwo or mbo level 2 diploma, your child must then keep learning until 18.

blocks.p: No one route suits every teenager. What suits a teenager depends on age, Dutch, school level at home, how long you stay, and the exams that come next. Here are the four routes parents ask about.

sections.h: ISK first, then regular secondary school

blocks.p: In the ISK your teenager learns Dutch and takes subjects like maths and citizenship. Then the pupil moves on to regular secondary school or mbo, with extra language help where needed. How it works, how to get a place and how long it lasts is in [newcomer classes and ISK](/guides/newcomer-classes-isk/). The law does not count Dutch language support as "extra support", so ask the school what it offers.

The ISK does not choose the track alone. A pupil from abroad has no Dutch school advice. The regular school looks at a doorstroomtoets if the pupil took one. If not, it may run its own suitability check. The school decides on admission and level. A pupil who turns 14 during that school year can also be admitted to year 1. Ask the ISK which schools its pupils usually move to, and when the planning starts. For a teenager of 14 or 15, the planning matters, because the exam years come soon.

blocks.say: Our son is 14 and will finish the ISK in about a year. How do you plan the move to a regular school and the level?

blocks.p: The Dutch school-leaving exams are taken in Dutch, also at a bilingual school. A bilingual school gives the regular Dutch diploma (vmbo, havo or vwo) and also a certificate that shows the extra language skills.

A pupil in an international school may study towards a different diploma. If your teen later wants to go to a Dutch university or college, check the entry rules for that diploma. Nuffic, the Dutch organisation for international recognition, can compare a foreign diploma with a Dutch one (a credential evaluation). It is not legally binding. With a complete application it usually takes at least 10 working weeks. Universities and universities of applied sciences decide on admission themselves.
School reports from home matter for placement, so bring them. See also [foreign diplomas](/questions/#foreign-diplomas) and the [system on one page](/system/).
Each track has a different length: vmbo is 4 years, havo 5 years and vwo 6 years, so the time to a diploma depends on the starting level and year.

Every child who lives in the Netherlands must go to school, whatever the nationality. This duty (leerplicht) ends at the end of the school year in which the child turns 16, or earlier after 12 full school years.

After that comes the qualification duty (kwalificatieplicht). Young people aged 16 and 17 who do not yet have a havo, vwo or mbo level 2 diploma (or higher) must keep going to school. They may not work full time. The mbo route that combines work and learning (bbl) counts. A pupil with a praktijkonderwijs diploma, or who leaves certain special education tracks, is exempt from this duty. Mbo has no tuition fee for students who are under 18 on 1 August. Books and materials may still cost money.

Mbo level 1 (the entry programme) needs no earlier diploma and is open once full-time compulsory schooling has ended. Levels 2 and 3 need a listed vmbo or mbo diploma, or proof that the pupil passed the first 3 years of havo or vwo. The official lists do not cover foreign diplomas, so ask the mbo school what it accepts. Nuffic can evaluate a foreign diploma.

If you live in the Netherlands and your child goes to school abroad, rules differ. For a school in Belgium or Germany you can ask your municipality's school attendance officer (leerplichtambtenaar) for an exemption, and you must report it again each year. Ask your municipality about other cases.

blocks.note: Unsure about the rules for a 16 or 17 year old? Ask the leerplicht department of your municipality. A school can also help.

sections.h: A Dutch teenager who comes back

blocks.p: A Dutch teen who returns after years abroad has the same duties and rights as any other child who lives here. The school looks at the school reports from abroad, and the school decides on year and level.
If the teen has lost much of their Dutch, ask the school and the municipality whether an ISK or extra Dutch lessons in a regular class are possible.
Do you plan your move? Contact the school before you arrive and ask what it needs. You can register during the school year. See [arriving mid-year](/questions/mid-year-arrival/).

steps: Collect school reports, a list of subjects, and the diploma or exam plan from the school at home.
Contact your municipality about newcomer places and ISK, or contact a secondary school directly. Do this before the move if you can.

Register in writing at more than one school, since classes can be full. If possible, do it at least 10 weeks before the start date you want. A school has 6 weeks to decide, and 4 more if it tells you it needs them.
Ask for the intake and ask who decides on the level.
Register with your municipality and get a BSN. See [BSN and address](/questions/bsn-and-address/).

blocks.p: To see the steps still ahead and the schools near you, enter your teenager's age and your postcode in the [route finder](/).
